We just finished a petal mosaic porch floor in Dover, MA. 265 square feet of Natucer Colonial porcelain in the Cotto color, a frost resistant extruded tile made in Spain. Two petal pieces and one kite make a module, and the modules lock into circles across the whole floor. Every one of those pieces went down loose, by hand, with no spacers. There is no spacer made for a curved petal or a four-point kite, so the joint between every piece is set by eye. If the gap drifts even a little from one side of the porch to the other, the circles stop reading as circles. The spacing has to hold from wall to wall. Before any tile went in, the floor got an uncoupling membrane. A three-season porch moves more than the inside of the house with temperature swings, and that layer keeps the movement from cracking tile or grout. Grout is Laticrete Parchment. Four bags for one porch, which tells you how much joint a floor like this has. This is the first of three porches in the house getting the same floor. If you have a porch, mudroom or floor tile installation in Dover or anywhere in Greater Boston, especially a shaped tile you have not seen installed before, we are happy to look at it.

From the owner
Planning a kitchen remodel in Orange County? The biggest mistake homeowners make isn't picking the wrong contractor, it's collecting quotes before they have a real budget. A proper plan starts with a hard ceiling based on your savings, financing capacity, and home equity, plus a contingency reserve of ten to fifteen percent for the surprises that almost always turn up once demolition starts. Most full remodels here land between forty five thousand and seventy thousand dollars, though projects range from twenty five thousand for basic updates to well over one hundred seventy five thousand for luxury builds. Once your ceiling is set, allocate spending by category, with cabinets and labor typically consuming the largest share, sometimes up to seventy five percent combined. Define your scope and layout before touching finishes, lock structural decisions early, and only request contractor quotes once your plan is solid, since quotes should confirm your numbers, not create them out of order. Comparing at least three itemized bids line by line, rather than total to total, reveals what's really included and what's been quietly left out. Protect your contingency fund for genuine hidden issues like outdated plumbing or electrical, not finish upgrades. When surprises hit mid-project, draw from contingency first, descope if needed, and document every change.

Fall is a smart time to start a basement finish in Boulder. Interior work isn’t affected by weather, so framing, electrical, and drywall can move along all winter. The one exception is egress window excavation, which is much easier before the ground freezes, so it’s worth scheduling early if you’re adding a bedroom. Permits can take a few weeks depending on the city, so starting the paperwork now keeps your timeline on track. Most basement finishes take six to ten weeks after permits, which means a project started now is typically done by midwinter. Insulation matters even more this time of year, and a well insulated basement stays comfortable without cranking the furnace. Ready to get your basement project on the calendar?
